title: Why do some people hate coriander?
subtitle: A taste of soap
subject: sciences
description: For part of humanity, coriander tastes like soap. The culprit: a single changed letter in a gene for smell, and perhaps a legacy from our ancestors.
author: stacy-jankowski

hero.hook: Same leaf, two flavors: fresh herb for some, soap for others. The difference comes down to one letter in your DNA.

blocks.text: Coriander is one of the oldest and most widely used plants in the world. The Greeks and Romans of antiquity were already growing it, for cooking and for medicine. It turns up in South Asia, in China, in Latin America, in thousands of recipes.

Yet some people cannot stand it. Where most diners taste a fresh herb, they swear they are chewing soap. It is neither fussiness nor a lack of habit: the answer lies in their nose, and more precisely in their genes.

sections.title: Olfactory receptors, from nose to brain

blocks.text: Everything you taste or smell has a chemical makeup that the brain must decode. Taste and smell, which scientists call [[olfaction]], are closely linked: much of the "flavor" of a dish actually travels through the nose, even while you are chewing.

blocks.caption: The olfactory nerve in the nasal cavity, on an anatomical plate from the early 20th century.

blocks.text: In the nasal cavity, cells carry [[olfactory receptors]]. They detect the molecules in food and turn them into a signal, which olfactory neurons carry to the brain. Each receptor is built from a gene. If that gene changes, the receptor changes too, and so does the flavor you perceive. That is exactly what happens with coriander.

Geneticists have identified the culprit: a gene called [[OR6A2]]. It codes for an olfactory receptor sensitive to [[unsaturated aldehydes]], molecules found in coriander. In most people, this receptor translates them into a fresh, herby note.

blocks.caption: The DNA double helix: a single changed letter is enough to alter a receptor.

blocks.text: Some people carry a [[single-nucleotide polymorphism]], or SNP, on this gene: one "letter" of the DNA is different. This tiny change alters how the gene is expressed, and therefore the receptor it produces. The receptor still works: it detects the molecule and sends a signal to the brain. But the message is no longer accurate. Instead of fresh herb, the brain reads: soap.

This variant does not appear at random in one individual. It has been passed down from parents to children for centuries. Depending on the region of the world, **4%** to **20%** of the population carries it. But why has such a trait persisted, when so many cuisines make coriander a staple?

blocks.caption: Mexican tacos with fresh coriander and lime: the herb sits at the heart of many cuisines.

blocks.text: Some evolutionary biologists offer a hypothesis. In the ancient world, certain toxic plants also gave off a soapy taste. A receptor that makes that taste repellent would have served as a survival mechanism, steering our ancestors away from dangerous plants. Harmless coriander would be collateral damage from this alarm signal.

sections.title: Can you learn to like coriander?

blocks.text: Good news for anyone dreaming of a proper taco: the brain can be retrained. The receptor itself will not change, but you can learn to ignore the signal it sends. The method comes down to one word: repetition.

In practice, you start by slipping a little coriander into a dish you already like. You can also mask the soapy note with a strong flavor, such as lemon juice or vinegar. After enough experiences with no unpleasant surprise, the brain comes to accept that coriander is not a threat, and the disgust fades.

Coriander's soapy taste comes from a variant of the OR6A2 gene, carried by 4 to 20% of humans depending on the region: their olfactory receptor misreads its aldehydes, perhaps an ancient protective reflex against toxic plants.

sources.text: N. Eriksson, S. Wu, C. B. Do et al., « A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference », Flavour, vol. 1, 2012, art. 22.
